KENYANG ORTHOGRAPHY GUIDE Tanyi Eyong Mbuagbaw Cameroon Association for Bible Translation and Literacy (CABTAL) B.P. 1299 Yaounde,́ Cameroon April, 1999 Abbreviations 1S First Person Singular 2S Second Person Singular 3S Third Person Singular 1P First Person Plural 2P Second Person Plural 3P Third person Plural 2 TABLE OF CONTENTS 3 KENYANG ORTHOGRAPHY GUIDE
The present work describes the orthography of Kenyang, a Bantoid language spoken in the Manyu and Meme Divisions of the South-West Province, Republic of Cameroon.
Kenyang has three main dialects: Upper Kenyang, Lower Kenyang and Kitwii.
Upper Kenyang and Lower Kenyang are situated in Manyu Division, and Kitwii in Meme Division.
Ittmann (1935/36) published the first research work in Kenyang, producing a grammar and a collection of folktales and proverbs.
In 1983, Tyhurst carried out a sociolinguistic study of Kenyang and Denya and analysed the phonology of Kenyang.
Mbuagbaw and Punches (1990) proposed the first tentative Kenyang alphabet and orthography.
The use of these materials over time by Kenyang speakers showed that there were certain inadequacies in the orthography and certain revisions were needed.
In 1996 the SIL Linguistics Department, together with speakers trained in reading and writing Kenyang, carried out research on the Kenyang tone system.
From a linguistic point of view, some of the problems presented by the Kenyang speakers were quite interesting.
The orthography problems were in two areas: First, there was the problem of marking tone, which the Kenyang speakers found difficult.
Secondly, there were problems concerning how best to represent certain word configurations.
Kenyang litearacy students felt that there were too many tone marks to learn and so their teachers requested a reduction in the number of tones that the students had to learn to read.
The teachers wanted only two tone marks, namely the high and rising ones.
These tones, according to the teachers, could easily be identified by the students.
Faced with this situation, Chris Jackson, Larry Seguin, and I investigated the situation and concluded that the orthography did need revision.
The Kenyang segmental alphabet is made up of twenty one consonants and nine vowels.
They are represented in upper and lower cases:
A a, B b, Bh bh, Ch ch, D d, E e, Ɛ ɛ, F f, G g, Gb gb, Gh gh, I i, Ɨ ɨ, J j, K k, Kp | kp, Mm, N n, Ŋŋ, Ny ny, O o, Ɔ ɔ, P p, R r, S s, T t, U u, Ʉ ʉ, W w, Y y.

Tyhurst (1984) and Mbuagbaw (1994) identified four basic tones in Kenyang: two level tones, high [́ ] and low [̀ ], and two contour tones, rising [̌ ] and falling [̂ ].
Tone was represented lexically within morphemes, and grammatically within sentences.
It is fairly easy to find Kenyang words where the only difference between them is tone.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: The grammatical functions of tones discussed above make it necessary to represent them in the Kenyang orthography.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Longacre (1964:136-7), Nida (1964b:26-7), and Wiesemann (1989:16) agree that when tone changes affect verb tenses and pronominal subjects, they should be marked in the orthography.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: In the 1990 orthography, tones were marked in the orthography as follows.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Since the low tone has a higher frequency than the high tone, the low tone was left unmarked, following the tone economy principle of Williamson (1984).

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: The other three tones were marked as high ( A ), falling ( _ ), and rising ( ' ).

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: The Society for Kenyang Literature (SKL) started producing literature in 1990 after the Linguistics Department of SIL, Yaoundé approved the initial tentative orthography.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: In 1991, the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA), financed the first teachers training seminar.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: About 55 teachers have now received training on how to teach Kenyang in their respective schools and communities, all using the initial orthography.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: After the teachers' seminar in 1991, teaching was started in various schools and community centres.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Beginning in 1995, we began receiving feedback from teachers and supervisors.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: One of the major problems was that of tone marking.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Many teachers shared the view that they did not see the difference between a downstepped high and a high tone on the one hand, and an unmarked low tone and a falling tone on the other hand.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: According to their suggestions, the downstepped high should have been marked as high, while the falling tone should have been left unmarked, like the low tone.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Following these suggestions, however, would cause important verbal contrasts to be neutralised, and thereby increase the level of ambiguity in the written forms.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: The reason was that the falling tone and the unmarked low mark a certain contrast in the verb stem.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: The same situation occurs between the high tone and the downstepped high.

(PROG) In order to solve these problems, Chris Jackson, an SIL member working with the Manyu team suggested that the grave accent from French could be used to mark the progressive aspect in Kenyang.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: We tried this proposal, and it has worked successfully Thus, instead of marking four tones, we mark only three and use the grave accent to indicate progressive aspect in the revised orthography.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Teaching the grave accent as the progressive aspect marker causes no problem for people used to the old orthography because the grave accent was previously not used in the old orthography.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: Mbuagbaw (1997) introduced this new system of marking tone in Kenyang Primer 1.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: A Teachers/supervisors seminar, organised in March, 1998, was a total success when the teachers received training with the new primer.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: The new system of marking tone and aspect was satisfactory to both the teachers and supervisors.

section: 3.3 Representation of Tone in the Orthography
content: They remarked that this orthography was easier than the first one because the number of tone marks was reduced from four to three, and the grave accent was only used with the progressive aspect.

Articles, negation markers, tense markers, and modal auxilliaries were written separately in the 1990 orthography as they are in English, and no attempt was made to determine the orthographic word in Kenyang from the native speaker's point of view.
Certain problems arose as to whether certain Èclitic typeÍ elements had the status of a word or not.
In the new orthography, the subject marker is attached to whatever follows it because linguistically, the subject marker is a verbal prefix similar in nature to the noun class prefix on nouns.

The noun phrase may consist of a head noun, followed by modifiers such as adjectives and/or determiners.
Noun phrases also include NP-NP constructions in which the first NP is ÈpossessedÍ by the second NP.
In Kenyang, this construction is marked by an associative marker between the possessor and the possessed.
Typical noun phrases are as follows: `chief's village' `pot of soup'

The associative phrase marker (henceforth AP) is a vowel in Kenyang.
For some noun classes it copies the final vowel of the first noun, and for other noun classes, the vowel is different.
The tone of the AP is either H or L, depending on the noun class of the head noun.

The imperative is taken as the citation form of the verb in this study.
The verb in Kenyang does not have a prefix or a suffix in its citation, or basic form.
The verb root in Kenyang is either monosyllabic, disyllabic or trisyllabic.
Kenyang distinguishes four tenses: near past, far past, future certain, and future uncertain; and four aspect markers: present perfective, present imperfective, present habitual, and the progressive.
In the orthography, the tense/aspect markers are written separately if they occur after the verb.
If they occur before the verb, they are written together with the preceding subject marker.

In the orthography, they are written as separate words. (20) Linguistic Form Orthographic Form Gloss fowl and fish `fowl and fish' 14 cap and book `cap and book' `He came then he ate.' Subordinators link dependent and independent clauses.
There are two types of subordinators, namely, subordinating conjunctions and subordinating adverbs.

The subordinating conjuctions in Kenyang are: mpok `when', m“bá k `if', kpá tɛ `until, and bɛ́ `that.' Subordinating adverbs include: kɛ `however', and yɛnɔ `nevertheless.' Subordinating adverbs are always followed by a comma in the orthography.

The comma in this case shows that a pause is obligatory. `However, they will not come tomorrow.' Yɛnɔ, mfɔ ǎ chɔŋ twɔ́ . `Nevertheless, the chief will come.' Most, if not, all modern orthographies include punctuation marks.
Unfortunately, in many literacy efforts, little effort is made to teach the functions and significance of each punctuation mark.
The reason for this is perhaps that they are regarded to be universal.

Gleason (1955:432) remarks that Èpeople do not expect to find differences in punctuation from language to language.Í Nevertheless, languages do differ sometimes in how they treat punctuation (e.g English vs French), and so we will now look at the conventions for punctuation in Kenyang.
The punctuation marks and the rules that govern them in Kenyang are the same as those for English.
The punctuation marks used for Kenyang are therefore as follows: 1) Full stop (.) 2) Question mark (?) 3) Exclamation mark ( ) 4) Comma (,) 5) Colon (:) 6) Semicolon (;) 7) Quotation marks (ÈÍ) 15
The full stop (.) in Kenyang marks the end of a declarative sentence: 3P.walk with legs `They are walking on foot.'
(23) Bá kɔ nɛ bɛkak.
The question mark (?) marks the end of an interrogative sentence Manyi 3S.buy.P1 what market `Manyi bought what in the market?' 3S.buy meat and beans `She bought meat and beans.'
(24) Má nyi aku yi ɛsyɛ́ ? | Aku nnya nɛ bako.
The exclamation mark marks either the end of a command, as in (25a), or is placed following exclamatory words or phrases, as in (25b).

It functions to express interjections, surprises, excitement, and forceful comments, as below. _Fn & `He should not come ' Chá expresses negative surprise, especially when one is accused of doing something of which he is unaware.
If there is an exclamation in the middle of a sentence, note that the word which follows the exclamation sign begins with a capital letter, as it is a new sentence.

16 Commas are used to indicate where a pause occurs or may occur in natural speech.
In oral communication, pauses always occur following certain grammatical units such as conjunctive adverbs.
The authors should note such pauses in a written text by inserting commas.

In Kenyang, the comma (,) serves several purposes: Words and Phrases Commas set off conjunctive adverbs that qualify or change the emphasis of a sentence. however chief 3S.NEG FUT come `However, the chief will not come.' Commas also set off contrasting words and phrases, no matter where they occur in a sentence.

Tambi NEG Tambɛ that 3S.die at.water `It wasTambi, not Tambe, that died in the stream.' 3P.NEG stay here 3P.stay FOC there `We do not live here, we live over there.' 3S.surpass years twenty 3S.be red and 3S.tall `He is more than twenty years old, red in colour, and tall.' Commas set off relative clauses.

In Kenyang, there is no difference between restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses. person who 3S.come here yesterday 3S.sick `The man, who came here yesterday, is sick.' village where stay.P1 FOC.

Tali `The village, where I stayed, was Tali.' Commas set off adverbial phrases and clauses when they occur at the beginning of sentences: when 2P.arrive.P1 Ndekwai Tambi and Tanyi 3P.go.P1 INF.stream `When we arrived Ndekwai, Tambi and Tanyi went to the stream.' 17 formerly P2 animals it.FOC P2 friendship `Formerly, animals were friends.' after nnywɔp ɛnɛ́ nfú (one day), day certain Tambe 3S.go hunting `One day, Tambe went hunting.' and after nkwɔ́ (also) at the beginning of a sentence, also when 3P.wash.P1 clothes 3P.give.P1 them food `Also, when they had finished washing clothes, they gave them food.'

Webster's Standard American Style Manual explains that a colon (:) introduces clauses that explain, illustrate, or restate what has gone before.

It is also used in dialogue or following a brief heading or an introductory term. 3S.like thing one food `She loves one thing: food.' The semicolon, on the other hand, pulls related sentences together.

Here are examples with a semicolon: When it pivots a contrast: do work time work play time play `Work when it is time to work; play when it is time to play.' between related independent clauses when the connection is omitted: 3S.cook.P1 good food yesterday one today it.good it.surpass `He prepared a nice meal yesterday; the one today is better.'

Quotation marks (ÈÍ) occur at the beginning and end of direct speech.
It has been argued that quotation marks are not needed in many African languages because some languages already employ quotative markers.
Though this is true, quotative marks only introduce the quoatation.
Koffi (1995:8) claims that there is no language where there is a lexical element which indicates the end of quotations.
If one relies on quotation openers only, one will not necessarily know when a given quotation ends.

To avoid such problems, it is better to use quotation marks that clearly indicate the beginning and end of quoted discourse, as below: 18 3S.ask.P1 2P.come.out where `He asked, ÈWhere are you from?' Quotation marks also set off special words, such as those that are not normally part of the language. thing that whitemen 3P.call that radio `The thing that whitemen call Èradio.Í' If the quotation needs a punctuation mark (question mark, exclamation mark, etc), it occurs before the last quotation mark. 3S.scream.P1 that come here `He screamed, ÈCome here Í' In general, all punctuations go inside quotations.

Capital letters are used at the beginning of sentences, proper nouns, and after a colon.

The first word in a declarative, interrogative, or exclamatory sentence is always capitalised, as below: First word in a sentence: 3P.go market evening this `They are going to the market this evening.' proper nouns: Tambi 3S.go school 3S.call.P1 Nso Ako Nkwa and Tiku `Tambi went to school and called the following: Nso, Ako, Nkwa, and Tiku.' after a colon: question it.FOC that 3S.come.P1 yesterday or 3S.NEG come.P1 `The question is: Did the chief come yesterday or not?' There are two main areas of change in the revised orthography.
The first is the tonal change (discussed under section 3.3.1).
The present system of marking tone reduces the number of tones which the speaker has to mark.
